title: Sub-30s LLM Pretraining on 8×H100? Modded-NanoGPT World Record Attempt (29.90 S)
content:
⚠️ This is a record attempt, built on other people's work. It is submitted as PR #406 (code) and PR #407 (runs and logs), and both are in review. It only becomes an official record if the maintainers verify it on their own hardware. All numbers below are from one rented 8×H100 node on runpod.io.
Modded-nanogpt is a community speedrun: train a GPT-2-scale language model from scratch on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs until it reaches a validation loss of 3.28 or lower, as fast as possible. Since 2024, dozens of contributors have taken that run from 45 minutes all the way down to around 30 seconds.
Three weeks ago, my second attempt hit 30.67 seconds (#396/#397). Since then, @caraxesml made another big jump with PR #404 — 30.25 seconds on GKE (and 30.05 seconds on our RunPod node).
That left the 30-second barrier just 50 milliseconds away.
This third attempt stacks cleanly on #404 with +175 net lines across 8 files. Same model, same data, same 1,053 training steps, and the exact same math — just less wasted GPU work. On the same 8×H100 node, it shaves off 145 milliseconds and crosses cleanly under 30 seconds at 29.90 seconds.
(Quick note on rules: this is Track 1, the standard from-scratch pretraining ruleset. Separate retrieval-hybrid tracks like #380 reach 5–10 seconds under different rules that allow exact lookups from training data.)
Standing on other people's work
Almost everything that makes this model fast comes from Keller Jordan (who started the speedrun), @francesco-prignano (PR #393), and @caraxesml (PR #404).
Because different cloud clusters run at slightly different speeds (#404 ran 30.25 s on GKE vs 30.05 s on our RunPod node), we timed #404 and our code back-to-back on the exact same machine.
Why "same math" can still run faster
Modern GPUs are extraordinarily fast at arithmetic, so they often spend their time waiting on memory traffic or tiny setup overheads rather than math. Two simple ideas account for most of our 145 ms gain:
Here are the six small fixes in PR #406 in plain English:
- One optimizer pass instead of two. The optimizer rescaled each weight row, wrote the result out to GPU memory, and immediately read it back to apply weight decay. Combining both into one compiled pass keeps the intermediate value in fast on-chip registers and cuts 61 GB of memory traffic:
# before (#404): write v_chunk out to GPU memory, then immediately read it back
v_chunk.mul_(eq_scale.type_as(v_chunk))
_sign_aligned_decay_update(p, mantissa, v_chunk, ...)
# after (#406): fuse both into one compiled pass (same bf16 rounding, zero round-trip)
update = (v_chunk * eq_scale.type_as(v_chunk)).float()
- Fill the full 128-byte memory line. When packing model weights down to 8-bit (FP8), the GPU was writing 64 bytes at a time — half of an H100's native 128-byte memory line. Widening the tiles to 128×128 fills the whole line in one write, and folding the scale calculation into the same kernel cuts extra launches.
- Skip an extra copy in the MoE optimizer. The model's specialist sub-networks (Mixture-of-Experts) were taking a slower optimizer path that made a separate copy of the weights. Moving them to the fast custom path and hiding that copy on idle GPU cores removes the extra step completely.
- Write 16-bit gradients directly. Gradients for the token-copying layer were written out as 32-bit floats and converted to 16-bit (bfloat16) in a second step. Casting them on the way out cuts memory traffic in half with identical bits:
# before (#404): store float32 temporaries, then cast to bf16 in a second pass
tl.store(DQ + offs, dq * scale)
return dq.to(q.dtype), dk.to(k.dtype)
# after (#406): cast on the way out — half the memory traffic, identical bits
tl.store(DQ + offs, (dq * scale).to(DQ.dtype.element_ty))
- Spread work evenly across all 132 GPU cores. A 4-line tile tweak (128×256 → 128×128) in the MoE backward pass creates twice as many independent work blocks, keeping all 132 compute units on each H100 busy instead of leaving some waiting.
- Warm up final-step kernels before the clock starts. PyTorch loads some GPU kernels lazily the first time a code path runs. Triggering the end-of-run weight-averaging path once during untimed setup keeps that one-time loading cost off the stopwatch.
The numbers
To rule out hardware drift, we ran 4 interleaved rounds on one RunPod 8×H100 node (1 × #404, then 3 × this PR), with random seeds and zero runs dropped:
- 145 ms faster than #404 on the exact same machine (p < 10⁻⁹), and 0.68 s faster than my previous #396 attempt.
- 12 out of 12 runs finished under 30.00 seconds and below the 3.28 loss target (p = 8.98 × 10⁻⁶).
- 45.0 Wh of GPU energy per run (5.42 kW across 8 GPUs at 72 °C max, zero throttling) — roughly the electricity needed to boil 400 ml of water in a kettle, down from 45.2 Wh on #404 and 45.6 Wh on #396.
What didn't work (and one win we threw away)
Half of our "clever" ideas failed once we measured them on real hardware. Testing every idea on a cheap single H100 pod first (about $2 total) saved hours of 8×H100 time:
- Three dense-MLP rewrites all ran slower — #393's kernel was already sitting at ~96% of the H100's hardware limit.
- Widening the attention-prep backward kernel crashed NVIDIA's GPU compiler (ptxas SIGSEGV).
- Sorting validation IDs on CPU looked tidy on paper, and accidentally added +537 ms before we caught and reverted it.
- We also threw away a working 10 ms win. An extra 132-line optimization pushed the run to 29.88 s (also passing n = 12, p = 0.0058), but we cut it from the PR to respect the repo's cleanliness rule: 132 lines for 10 ms isn't worth the complexity.
What's next
A final GPU profile of our winning run shows roughly 10% of GPU time still goes to multi-GPU communication (gradient exchanges and n-gram lookups). Trimming or overlapping more of that looks like the cleanest path toward 29 seconds flat.
Thanks to Keller Jordan for the speedrun, @francesco-prignano for #393, and especially @caraxesml for #404. Even if #406/#407 doesn't hold up on maintainer hardware, breaking 30 seconds on a rented node — and seeing which ideas survived reality — was a lot of fun.
ℹ️ How this attempt was made
I used Google Antigravity with Gemini agents running in parallel for GPU profiling, Triton/PyTorch kernel work, single-GPU parity checks, RunPod provisioning, and clean zero-interference 8×H100 runs.
Development and dead-end screening ran on single H100 pods (about $2), followed by 2 hours 48 minutes on one 8×H100 SXM node on RunPod for the interleaved certification runs and final profile. Every run is counted, and every log embeds the exact source code that produced it.
The submission, its claims and any mistakes are mine.
Best Regard,
Amund

report.summary: Amund's PR #406 cuts 145 ms off modded-nanogpt's record, training a GPT-2-scale model to loss 3.28 in 29.90 s on 8×H100 — pending maintainer verification.
report.background: Modded-nanogpt is a community 'speedrun' started by Keller Jordan in 2024: train a GPT-2-scale language model from scratch on 8 NVIDIA H100s until validation loss hits 3.28, as fast as possible. Since then, dozens of contributors have pushed the record from roughly 45 minutes down to about 30 seconds — a compression that mirrors the broader maturation of the LLM stack, where most near-term gains now come from systems engineering rather than new architectures. Amund's prior attempt hit 30.67 s; contributor @caraxesml's PR #404 reached 30.05 s on the same rented RunPod node, leaving the sub-30-second barrier just 50 ms away. The attempt sits in 'Track 1' — standard from-scratch pretraining — as distinct from retrieval-hybrid tracks that reach 5-10 s under looser rules allowing exact lookups from training data. Everything runs on a rented 8×H100 node, and the record only counts once maintainers reproduce it on their own hardware.
key_points: Same math, less wasted silicon: the run keeps the identical model, data, 1,053 steps and numerics as PR #404. The 145 ms gain comes purely from eliminating redundant memory traffic, such as fusing the optimizer's rescale and weight-decay steps into one pass — saving 61 GB of read/write traffic by keeping intermediate values in on-chip registers.

Six micro-fixes, memory-first: packing FP8 weights into full 128-byte H100 memory lines instead of 64-byte half-writes, storing gradients directly in bfloat16 instead of float32-then-cast, and retuning a tile from 128×256 to 128×128 so all 132 GPU cores stay busy in the MoE backward pass.

Overhead hunting counts: two fixes target pure setup cost — routing Mixture-of-Experts weights through the fast custom optimizer path, and pre-triggering lazily loaded PyTorch kernels during untimed warmup so one-time compilation never lands on the stopwatch.

Statistical rigor, not a lucky run: four interleaved rounds of #404 versus the new code on the exact same node, random seeds, zero runs dropped. All 12 runs finished under 30.00 s and below the loss target (p < 10⁻⁹ versus #404), with 45.0 Wh of GPU energy per run.

Most ideas failed: three dense-MLP rewrites ran slower because PR #393's kernel already sat at ~96% of hardware peak, one kernel crashed NVIDIA's ptxas compiler, and a working 10 ms win was discarded because 132 extra lines weren't worth the repo's cleanliness bar.
report.impact: This is a small record with a large signal: at GPT-2 scale on H100s, arithmetic is essentially free and the bottleneck is memory movement and launch overhead. Techniques showcased here — kernel fusion, memory-line-aligned FP8 packing, cast-on-store gradients, occupancy-aware tile sizing, warmup off the clock — are exactly the levers that transfer to production pretraining and inference, where the same bandwidth walls dominate. For developers, the run is a template for methodology: screen ideas on a $2 single-GPU pod, then certify on an 8-GPU node with interleaved A/B runs and seeded statistics, and keep logs that embed the source code. For regular users the payoff is indirect but real — cheaper, faster training and lower energy per run, plus a public benchmark showing where optimization effort actually pays off versus where hardware is already saturated.
report.tools: Follow the modded-nanogpt repo (Keller Jordan) and read PRs #393, #404, #406/#407 for the actual kernels. The work is written in PyTorch with custom Triton kernels, profiled with NVIDIA Nsight Compute; RunPod supplies the 8×H100 node. The author used Google Antigravity with parallel Gemini agents for profiling and kernel iteration, plus ~$2 single-H100 pods for dead-end screening. For comparable large-scale references, watch llm.c, torchtitan and NanoGPT.
